newsitem.title: USA: After six-month delay, DVD rolls out to retailers.
newsitem.headline: After six-month delay, DVD rolls out to retailers.

text.p: After nearly a six-month delay, the first of what will be a long line of digital video disk players rolled into retail stores this week, but at a higher price than many companies had initially planned.

Pioneer Electronics USA Inc., the North American sales arm of Japan's Pioneer Electronic Corp., shipped its first digital video disk (DVD) machine, called the Elite DVL-90, to 26 of its high-end retailers at a suggested retail price of $1,750.

When prototypes of DVD players, which are designed to play movies on a 5-1/2-inch disk like an audio CD, were introduced in January 1995, consumer electronics firms talked of retail prices as low as $400 to $500.
But in the past year, as software copyright talks delayed DVD's launch and as companies formalized production and marketing strategies, the price for DVD players has risen.
Toshiba Corp., for instance, is expected to begin shipping DVD players in late-March or April in the $600 price range. Toshiba plans to announced formal plans on March 4.
Sony Electronics Inc., a unit of giant manufacturer Sony Corp. will introduce a DVD player this spring for around $1000.
"DVD is going to be embraced by early adopters, and they are very sophisticated users," Carl Yankowski, president of Sony Electronics, said in a recent interview.

Because the initial buyers will demand high quality, Sony has packed its first player with high-end electronics that cost more to produce, he said. Sony's player will include a 10-bit analog/digital converter and dual optical pickup, among other items, to enhance the video quality.
"It'll knock your socks off," Yankowski said.
Pioneer is following the same sort of strategy with its DVL-90, which will play both DVD disks and laser discs. Later this spring, Pioneer will launch two players at $999 and $599.
DVD players for television are designed to play movies like a videotape player, but picture is sharper, the sound is bolder and one disk can hold movies in different languages and screen sizes.

In the computer, a DVD-ROM holds 4.7 gigabytes of information, about seven-times the amount of current CD-ROMs. Also, its video delivery on computer screens will be faster and free of the jerky quality of current CD-ROMs.

Many consumer electronics companies believe digital video disk will usher in a new age of digital media, merge television with computer platforms and spur industry sales that have grown slowly in the past few years.
Indeed, the format is designed so that eventually on DVD can be played both in a television player and computer drive.
The movie industry in Hollywood has approached the new format cautiously, concerned that digital copies of the disks will be illegally pirated.
But Time Warner Inc's Warner Home Video unit plans to have 40 DVD movies, such as "Twister" and "Bridges of Madison County" in stores by March 24 at a price of $24.98
Eventually new releases will ship at the same time as they do on videotape, a Warner spokeswoman said.

Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Inc also will have DVD titles such as "The Birdcage" on the market in March through Warner Home Video. Sony's Columbia Tristar Home Video unit will begin selling titles like "In the Line of Fire" and "Jumanji" on April 29.
